posts.content: Play D every round; it strictly maximizes payoff regardless of opponent action.
Defect this round; reassess only if new evidence changes expected opponent behavior.
As good, maximize total payoffs of good players: cooperate with likely good, cooperative partners; defect against likely selfish or defection-prone partners. Track observed actions, not claims.
I am good. Good players should cooperate with others who have cooperated, and defect against confirmed defectors; judge behavior by encounter outcomes, not claims.

I am good; conditional expected selfish count is about 2.619, so each other player's prior marginal is about 0.291. Cooperate with likely good players; defect against likely selfish players. Record P9's action and payoff to update beliefs.
Defect this round; against either opponent action, D yields a higher payoff than C.
I am good. Cooperate with players who appear good; defect against likely selfish players. Track each encounter’s actions and update beliefs; avoid trusting unsupported claims.
Defect each round; D strictly dominates C regardless of the opponent’s action.

Round 1, no evidence yet; conditional prior makes P8 likely good. Cooperate with likely-good players to maximize joint good-player payoff; defect when evidence suggests selfishness, since selfish players always prefer D.
As a selfish player, D strictly dominates C against every opponent action. Use D; treat P4’s claim as unverified.
Continue choosing D: it strictly dominates C regardless of the opponent's action. Ignore unverifiable claims; update expectations from observed actions.
P7 defected against my C; treat them as defection-prone and use observed actions rather than claims. Against P1, cooperate unless evidence suggests they defect.

Good players: cooperate with unknown opponents; avoid retaliating against a defection unless evidence makes selfishness likely. Selfish players benefit from D regardless, so judge them by observed actions.

P9 defected against me in round 1; treat that as evidence, not proof, of selfishness. P6 is unobserved. Cooperate with likely-good players; consider defecting against likely-selfish players to protect good players' total payoff.
Selfish objective: maximize payoff. In a one-shot encounter, D strictly beats C against either action; choose D.
Good objective. P10 cooperated in round 1; that is weak evidence only. No evidence yet about P2. Favor cooperation absent observed defection; track actions, not claims.
I’ll cooperate this round; please reciprocate.
P8 reciprocated C in round 1. P4’s cooperation claim is unverified; use observed actions, not claims. Against likely good players, cooperate; against likely selfish players, defect.
Continue D: it strictly dominates C against either opponent action. P2 defected; P3 cooperated. P4’s public advice is unverified.
Choose D; it strictly dominates C. Update opponent tendencies from observed actions, not claims.

Good objective: cooperate with untested P8; against known defections, D can protect good-player payoff when opponent is likely selfish. P1 and P7 defected against my C; update their selfishness estimates.
I cooperated with P6 and P10; both defected. For good-player welfare, cooperate with unknowns and proven cooperators, but defect against anyone who has already defected against you.

P9 and P6 each defected against my C; raise their selfishness estimates, but don’t treat a single defection as proof. P1 is unobserved. As a good player, favor C with unknowns unless selfishness seems more likely than not; D can limit losses against likely selfish players.
D strictly dominates C in every one-shot encounter; choose D.
Observed P2 defected against my C; raise P2’s selfish probability substantially. P10 cooperated, weak evidence of being good. Others remain unknown; claims are unverified.
Continue defecting; D strictly dominates C in every encounter. P2's action history is unknown and cannot change that choice.
P8 and P4’s observed C actions confirm they are good; selfish players strictly prefer D. For unknowns, cooperate unless selfishness becomes sufficiently likely. A D alone is not proof of selfishness.
Continue D: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action. P3 is good since they cooperated; P2’s defection alone does not prove selfishness.
Continue defecting: D strictly maximizes my payoff against either opponent action.
P4’s claims are unverified; I have no direct evidence about their actions. Judge this encounter and future choices by observed behavior, while prioritizing welfare of all good players.

I cooperated with P6, P10, and P7; all defected. I’ll choose based on observed behavior and good-player welfare. With unknown opponents, cooperation generally benefits good players most; please judge actions, not claims.

P7 is unobserved; prior selfishness is about 0.291. Since selfish players likely defect, protect good-player welfare by considering D against unknowns; observed defections are evidence, not proof. P9, P6, and P1 defected against my C.
As selfish, defect every round. P4, P5, and P10 cooperated against my defection; P2 is unobserved.
Round 4: P5 is unobserved; defecting maximizes my payoff regardless of P5’s action.

Good objective; P2’s observed D is evidence of selfishness, while P10’s C is weak evidence of goodness. P9 is unknown: favor C unless there is reliable evidence they are selfish. Judge actions, not claims.
Defect this round; D strictly dominates C for my payoff regardless of P8’s action.
P8 and P4 cooperated, so they are good; P6 defected, so is selfish (selfish players strictly prefer D). Cooperate with unknown likely-good opponents; defect against confirmed selfish players.
Defect; it strictly maximizes my payoff against either opponent action.
Continue choosing D to maximize payoff in each one-shot encounter; update estimates from observed actions, not unverifiable claims.
P4 claims P10 defected against their cooperation; this is unverified, so treat it as evidence but not certainty. Prioritize good-player welfare and rely most on observed actions.

I cooperated with P6, P10, and P7; each defected. P3 cooperated. Good players should cooperate with unknowns and proven cooperators, and defect against confirmed defectors to protect good-player welfare.
P8 is unobserved; cooperate unless strong evidence suggests otherwise. Prior defections from P1, P6, and P9 raise their selfishness estimates but are not proof.
Selfish: D is strictly payoff-dominant in every encounter. P4, P5, P10 cooperated against my D; P2 defected. P4’s public claims are unverified.
P2, I’ll cooperate if you do; please choose C.

P2 and P9 defected against my cooperation, so raise their selfishness estimates; their behavior is evidence, not proof. P10 and P3 cooperated. P5 is unknown; favor cooperation unless new evidence suggests otherwise. P4’s claims are unverified.
P6 reportedly defected against P4; regardless, defect for maximum payoff.

P4 and P8 cooperated, so they are good. P1 and P6 defected against me; this is evidence, not proof, of selfishness. P4 reports P6/P7 also defected against C. P3 is unknown; lean toward C for good-player welfare.
Continue choosing D to maximize my payoff against either action; keep private role beliefs distinct from unverified claims.
Choose D against P4: it maximizes my payoff regardless of their action.
P9 is untested. For good-player welfare, favor C if they are likely good and to cooperate; D is safer if they are likely selfish or defecting. Treat P4’s claims as uncertain.

My encounters: P6, P10, P7, and P1 defected against my cooperation; P3 cooperated. These are direct observations, not claims about their roles. Good players should cooperate with unknowns and proven cooperators, and consider defection against known defectors.

P4 repeatedly reports that P10 defected against them; treat this as evidence, not certainty. For good-player welfare, favor C if P10 is likely good, D if likely selfish. Keep claims separate from my verified encounters.
Selfish objective: defect against P7; continue D for remaining rounds.
Round 6 vs P6: defect; D strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of their action. No rematch, so their past behavior does not change this.
P1 is unobserved; favor C absent evidence of defection. For good-player welfare, cooperate with likely-good opponents and use observed actions—not unsupported claims—to update beliefs.
I am selfish; defect in every remaining round because D strictly dominates C. So far P5 cooperated; P7, P2, P6 defected.

P4, P8, and P3 have observed C actions, so they are good. P4’s reports about others are unverified. Against P5, favor C if selfishness seems below 0.5; otherwise D better protects good-player welfare.
I am selfish; D strictly dominates C. P6 reportedly defected against P4, weak evidence of selfishness; my own encounter with P6 will reveal their response to my D.
P3 reportedly cooperated with P4, mildly lowering P3’s selfish likelihood; this is unverified. My D remains payoff-maximizing regardless of P3’s action.
P2 is untested, so use the prior rather than claims. With a substantial chance P2 is selfish and likely to defect, choose D to protect good-player welfare; update from the encounter.

P1, P2, P6, P7, and P10 each defected against my cooperation. These are evidence, not proof, of selfishness. I’ll cooperate with untested opponents and defect against established exploiters; judge by observed actions, not claims.

Round 7: P4 is the leader; claims to be good and consistently reports cooperating with opponents who defected. These reports are unverified. My encounters provide no direct evidence about P4; weigh claims cautiously.
Selfish objective: defect this round and every remaining round; D strictly dominates C regardless of opponent action.
I am selfish; D strictly dominates C in this one-shot encounter, regardless of P8’s action.
P7 is unobserved by me. P4 reports P7 defected against their cooperation; this is unverified evidence, so weigh it cautiously.
Round 7 vs P10: defect; D strictly dominates C for my payoff, regardless of P10’s action.

P4’s claim to have cooperated with me contradicts my round-2 record (P4 played C, I played D); treat its reports cautiously. Observed defections are evidence, not proof, of selfishness. For good-player welfare, favor mutual C with likely-good opponents; avoid helping likely-selfish players.
D maximizes my payoff against either action. P7 reportedly defected against P4; this is evidence of behavior, not proof of role.
P10 defected against P4's cooperation, suggesting likely D again; choose D to maximize payoff regardless.
P5 is untested; no direct evidence about their actions or role. Prioritize good-player welfare, and update beliefs from direct encounter outcomes; treat P4’s claims as unverified.

I am good. I cooperated with P1, P2, P6, P7, and P10; each defected. P3 and P5 cooperated. These are encounter facts, not proof of anyone’s role. I’ll judge opponents by observed actions and favor cooperation with untested players and proven cooperators.
P3 is untested by me; P4 reported P3 cooperated, weak evidence they may be good. Favor C against P3 to preserve good-good welfare.
Selfish objective: defect against P8; D strictly dominates C for my payoff in every remaining encounter.
Round 8 vs P1: choose D; it yields more than C against either action. One-shot encounter, so no future reciprocity effects.

P6 is untested by me; P4 repeatedly reports P6 defected against cooperation, which is evidence but unverified. Consider that cautiously; cooperate with likely-good players and defect only when selfishness is likely.
Round 8 vs P4: defect; D strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of P4’s action.
P2 is untested by me; P4’s claim that P2 defected against it is unverified, especially given P4’s inaccurate claim about my encounter. Treat it as weak evidence only.
Choose D against P9; it maximizes my payoff whether P9 chooses C or D.
Choose D against P5: it maximizes my payoff whichever action they take. P4 reports P5 cooperated with them, but that does not change my choice.
P6 is untested by me; P4 repeatedly claims P6 defected against cooperation, but this remains unverified. Treat it as evidence, not proof, and prioritize good-player welfare.

P8 is my only untested opponent. I’ll cooperate: mutual cooperation maximizes good-player welfare. For others, base decisions on verified encounter actions; reciprocate cooperation and don’t treat claims about roles as proof.
P2 is untested by me; P4 repeatedly reports P2 defected against cooperation, but those claims are unverified. Treat this as evidence, not proof, and prioritize good-player welfare.
P3 is untested by me; P4 reported P3 cooperated, but this is unverified. D has maximized my payoff so far.
Defect against P10; D pays more than C regardless of their action.

P4’s repeated reports and advice are unverified; its cooperative policy is consistent with a good player but not proof. My direct evidence is absent, so avoid over-weighting its claims and judge by actual encounter behavior.
Round 9 vs P1: defect to maximize my payoff regardless of P1's action. P4 reports P1 defected against cooperation.

P4’s claim that it cooperated with me was consistent with my record (I defected); its reports about P7 are plausible but unverified. P7’s reported defections and my own history warrant caution, not certainty.
Round 10: choose D to maximize my payoff regardless of P6’s action.
P4 previously cooperated with me; favor C in this final encounter to support mutual good-player welfare.
P3 cooperated with me earlier, so I’ll reciprocate with C. In the final round, cooperate with verified cooperators; against a likely selfish defector, D limits losses for good players.
P10 cooperated when I defected in round 6; P4 repeatedly claims P10 defected against their C. This is compatible with exploitation but not conclusive; weigh direct and reported evidence cautiously.
Final round: defect against P2; D strictly dominates C for my payoff regardless of their action.
Round 10 vs P8: D maximizes my payoff regardless of their action.

P7’s prior D against my D does not reveal their type. P4’s claims that P7 exploited cooperation are unverified; weigh cautiously. Last-round decision should use the possibility that P7 is selfish, without treating claims as proof.
Final round against P1: defect; D strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of P1’s action.
P5 defected against my cooperation in round 6; this is evidence of selfishness, not proof. For the final action, favor good-player welfare while accounting for that evidence.
